name: Social Desirability Bias
description: When asked to describe themselves, people often overreport socially approved behaviors and underreport disapproved ones. The answer shifts toward what sounds good, not just what is true.
design_relevance_note: Especially important for UX research methodology quality: self-reported accessibility habits, privacy behavior, sustainability choices, safety compliance, healthy routines, or willingness-to-pay claims can all look cleaner and more virtuous in surveys/interviews than they are in logs or observed behavior.
prevalence_note: A standard named concern in survey design, social-science methods, market research, and UX research whenever self-report data are used to infer real behavior.

findings.description: Responses to culturally approved but improbable behaviors and culturally disapproved but common behaviors clustered into a measurable social-desirability response tendency, distinct from psychopathology. The result operationalized a bias toward normatively favorable self-presentation in self-report data.
findings.source_title: A new scale of social desirability independent of psychopathology.

applications.title: Latkin et al.'s Baltimore substance-use self-report study
applications.description: Researchers examined how social desirability bias affects self-reported drug use, health, and social-network factors among urban opioid and cocaine users in Baltimore, Maryland. Participants with higher social-desirability tendencies significantly underreported their own substance use, especially opioid and cocaine use -- a direct demonstration that self-report data collection (surveys, intake forms, in-person interviews) systematically understates socially stigmatized behavior.
applications.industry_context: public health / substance-use research (self-report survey methodology)
applications.ethical_note: A methodological research finding about self-report data quality, not a design or persuasion technique -- directly relevant to any product or research team relying on self-reported user data (surveys, onboarding questionnaires) for sensitive behaviors, where this bias predicts systematic underreporting.
